texts.orig: Abstract The integrity assessment of nuclear reactor pressure tubes (PTs) used in pressurized heavy water reactors necessitates the determination of their tensile property data. This in turn will require the employment of appropriate specimens that can be fabricated from them. If this is to be done on the material in the irradiated condition it will be essential to resort to sub-size or miniature sized specimens which need to be designed and tested to prove its efficacy in providing the correct output. With this aim in view two different sheet type tensile specimens were designed for estimating the tensile property data of both axial and circumferential directions of the PT. A370 and tested as per ASTM Std. E8. Thus the output generated from the axial sheath tensile specimens would serve the purpose of providing standard and reliable tensile property data of the material and that too at the component level. texts.orig: Pressurized heavy water reactors (PHWRs) are the mainstay of Indian nuclear power programme. Zirconium based alloys are widely used in these reactors as materials for ding for the fuel elements. These alloys have very low neutron absorption cross-section and excellent corrosion resistance besides the properties of good compatibility with the coolant and fuel along with adequate mechanical properties.
texts.text: Pressurized heavy water reactors (PHWRs) are the mainstay of Indian nuclear power programme. Zirconium based alloys are widely used in these reactors as materials for ding for the fuel elements. These alloys have very low neutron absorption cross-section and excellent corrosion resistance besides the properties of good compatibility with the coolant and fuel along with adequate mechanical properties.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The PTs of Indian PHWRs are made up of zirconium alloys such as Zircaloy-2 (in older type of reactors) and Zr-2.5 % Nb (in newer type of reactors especially from Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS) onwards) [1]. These tubes carry fuel bundles which contain the natural uranium dioxide fuel inside the fuel pins/elements. These tubes are of 82 mm diameter (internal) and have a wall thickness of 4.3 mm approximately in the case of Zircaloy2 and 3.6 mm for Zr-2.5 % Nb type. The tubes are normally subjected to internal pressure of 10.3 MPa and temperature of 300 ° C approximately during the reactor operation in addition to the radiation and corrosive environment. It is essential to ensure the integrity of the PT so as to assure the safe operation of the reactor as it is a primary pressure boundary material in the PHWR system. Such an assessment becomes all the more important because the severe conditions of pressure, temperature, radiation and corrosive environment experienced by them during their prolonged service life in the reactor would considerably affect their operational efficiency thereby making them unable to carry out the intended function after a certain period [2-9]. The integrity assessment of the PT would make it necessary to estimate their mechanical properties (i.e. yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and ductility) periodically.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The estimation of mechanical property data would primarily call for suitable test specimens to be made available. Extraction of standard test specimens out of an irradiated PT would be a tall order in view of the radiation hazard associated with it. Under such scenario, the availability of miniature sized tensile specimens would be a welcome solution. However, the results obtainable from these specimens will require to be calibrated against standard conventional specimens. Further, zirconium and its alloys have a hexagonal close packed structure due to which their mechanical properties would differ in the longitudinal and transverse directions. The anisotropic effect is further enhanced by the processing the material is subjected to during the special fabrication route it goes through. The nuclear PTs and cladding tubes are fabricated in India by pilgering technology-a process in which high reduction in thickness and diameter can be simultaneously achieved so as to provide adequate mechanical properties to them with relative ease. All these aspects make it necessary to determine the mechanical behaviour of the zirconium alloy component in both the directions of loading, i.e. longitudinal and transverse.

texts.orig: In order to achieve the above cited objective it would be required to evolve suitable alternative methodologies that would provide reliable and correct mechanical properties of PTs especially in the irradiated condition. This will make it essential to establish the applicability of such methodologies initially in the unirradiated condition of the component under investigation so as to gain adequate confidence to make use of the same approach subsequently when the component is in irradiated condition also. The paper furnishes the outcome of an experimental approach that was adopted to tackle the problem. It also discusses the major considerations involved in designing the various types of tensile specimens utilized for the investigation.

texts.orig: A bunch of 18 number of sheath type tensile specimens having the full thickness of the PT were extracted from the PT in the axial direction in such a way that the length of each specimen coincided with that of the axis of the tube. Figure 2a illustrates pictorially the approach adopted in the fabrication of the sheath specimens. The slitting of the specimens was accomplished by using electric discharge machining (EDM) technique so as to provide specimens of accurate dimensions which were free from burs, dimensional errors, rounded ends etc. The circumferential spacing of each specimen was designed/adjusted such that two diagonally opposite specimens would result from one single slitting along the length of the tube. Adopting this procedure would make it feasible to secure 18 numbers of sheath specimens (having a width of 12.5 mm) to be sliced out of a 75 mm long tubular piece belonging to PT.

This problem occurred primarily in the case of fabricating the transverse tensile specimen wherein the thickness of the proposed plate sample was required to be obtained only from the available flat portion that could be sliced out of the curved section of a tubular piece. This information was successfully derived by applying engineering drawing which furnished the maximum length of the blank having the required thickness that could be extracted out of a given curved piece which had the same width as that of the specimen. texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the case of fabrication of an axial plate tensile specimen, it was decided to design it in such a way that all its basic dimensions like the width and thickness at the gauge length region would be identical to those of the circumferential plate specimen except the total length. This was done due to four reasons: (1) There is not much difficulty in getting the required flat blanks of any length in the axial direction, (2) It is also possible to get a flat blank (which can be later converted into a tensile specimen) of any thickness like 2-3 mm in the axial direction, (3) If the total length alone was increased it would help in evolving straight comparison of the test results as the critical dimensions are unaltered, (4) Increasing the total length of the axial specimen would help in avoiding the likely mixup while fabricating a large number of specimens. Thus the total length of an axial plate tensile specimen was kept about 30 mm as displayed in Fig. 1b. The manner of extracting such specimens is brought out clearly in Fig. 2c. It is evident from this figure that many axial specimens can be sliced out of a given tubular piece.

texts.orig: The reliability, accuracy and correctness of tension test data that can be generated would depend upon many factors like how well the specimens have been designed, the fabrication procedure followed, the uniformity in the dimensions of the test specimen especially its thickness, the type of grips & fixtures employed, the compliance of the loading system, the firmness with which the specimen is held within the grips without spoiling it, the manner in which the specimen is aligned within the grips, how well the set consisting of the of the specimen, the grips & fixtures are aligned with respect to the load line of the testing machine, the testing speed used and its consistency in the machine, the quality of the testing machine put to use, the accuracy in the calibration of the load cells etc. Out of the variety of factors listed above, the three most important points within our control are the consistency in the dimensions of the specimen, method of fabricating the sample, the type of grips & fixtures employed for the experiment as all other factors are expected to be of standard quality. Of the three important criteria mentioned above, the first two have been already taken into consideration in the present work as described earlier. With regard to the third point concerning that of the grips & fixtures utilized for the test, a new set was specially designed for carrying out the testing of the miniature tensile specimens fabricated as described earlier. Figure 3 shows a photograph of the grips & fixtures designed and fabricated for carrying out tension test of plate type tensile specimens.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The grips are special in the sense that they have been designed specifically for conducting the tension test of miniature plate tensile specimen without damaging it either before testing or during the test. The set of grips & fixtures is special also because of the fact that the test specimen can be easily engaged in them and tightened firmly with minimum effort and hence can be used for remote handling purposes when a need arises for testing radioactive specimens. Also the design of the grips & fixtures is such that they can be easily attached to the cross heads of the testing machine and clamped with the help of loading pins which will faithfully transmit the load from the load cell to the specimen in a uni-axial manner which is the prime requisite of the tension test.

texts.orig: The tests were carried out at room temperature using a screw-driven universal testing machine (UTM) at a crosshead speed of 0.25 mm/min for all the types of specimens fabricated. The sheath tensile specimens were tested by engaging them one at a time in the readily available standard Wedge Action type of Grips. Each one of the samples was pre-loaded to 4,000 N prior to testing in order to take off the slackness existing in the load line. The plate/sheet type of tensile specimens were tested by making use of the special set of grips & fixtures designed and fabricated for the purpose. In this case a preload of 300 N was applied to the test sample.

texts.orig: The dimensions of thickness and width of the specimen at the parallel region were measured a few times before engaging it within the respective grips. Extreme care was exercised in properly aligning the entire assembly consisting of specimen & grips with the adaptors which had been attached to the load line to complete the load train before starting the test. No extensometer was attached to any of the samples before testing. This was done with a view to simulating the method that would be followed during the testing of radioactive samples also as it would not be a feasible proposition. Moreover, the design of the sample did not take into account the need to provide additional length necessary for fixing an extensometer onto it in view of the same logic connected with remote handling difficulties.

texts.orig: Table 3a and b shows the room temperature test results generated by making use of Zr-2 axial sheath tensile specimens belonging to PT and Zr-2 axial plate tensile specimens respectively from the same PT. The average values of 0.2 % YS obtained were 493 and 486 MPa respectively while those in the case of UTS were 595 and 618 MPa respectively. The uniform and total ductility values for the sheath type specimens were (6.8, 20.35 %) while those obtained from miniature plate tensile specimens were (7.67, 20.6 %). These test results are within the range of experimental error. texts.orig: The earlier discussion had clearly brought out the fact that it would be possible to get reliable and consistent tensile property data of Zr-2 and Zr-2.5 % Nb materials by making use of miniature plate tensile specimens as well as sheath tensile specimens for the axial direction of the respective tubes. Thus the one-to one correspondence between the two types of specimens clearly had got established primarily for the axial direction of both the tubes. In view of that reasoning it can be logically assumed that it would be equally appropriate to consider the use of only miniature plate tensile specimens fabricated from the circumferential direction of the same tubes for determining their transverse tensile property data. Hence, it can be argued with adequate conviction that it is possible to make use of miniature plate tensile specimens alone for the determination of tensile property data of the two important materials, namely Zr-2 and Zr-2.5 % Nb alloys available in the form of tubular geometry.
